blocks.text: In a reflexive verb the action comes back to the person who does it. The infinitive ends in -se: levantarse (to get up), llamarse (to be called). Before the conjugated verb you add a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject.

blocks.label: reflexive · regular -ar
examples: They are called Luis and Marta.

blocks.label: reflexive · regular -ar
examples: What time do you get up?
Do you (all) get up late on Sundays?

blocks.title: Formal: ¿Cómo se llama usted?
blocks.text: To ask a stranger or an older person their name, use usted: ¿Cómo se llama usted? To introduce yourself, Me llamo… or Soy… both work.
2. Reflexive verbs that change their stem
Many reflexive verbs are boot verbs (PDF 3): the stem changes in yo, tú, él and ellos but not in nosotros and vosotros.

blocks.title: Regular reflexive verbs for your daily routine

blocks.text: Me despierto a las siete, me ducho, desayuno y salgo de casa a las ocho. Por la noche me acuesto a las once. (I wake up at seven, take a shower, have breakfast and leave the house at eight. At night I go to bed at eleven.)

blocks.title: Body parts and clothes: use el, la, los, las
blocks.text: Dutch says ik was mijn handen. Spanish uses the article, not a possessive: Me lavo las manos, Me pongo el abrigo. The reflexive pronoun already shows whose hands they are.

blocks.title: Reflexive or not?
blocks.text: Compare lavo el coche (I wash the car) with me lavo (I wash myself), and acuesto al niño (I put the child to bed) with me acuesto (I go to bed). Many verbs exist in both forms.

Gustar works backwards compared with English or Dutch. What you like is the subject and the person who likes it is the indirect object. Me gusta el café means coffee is pleasing to me. So the verb agrees with the thing liked: gusta for one thing or an infinitive, gustan for several things.

head: Who likes it
Pronoun
one thing / an activity
several things
rows: Me gusta el café. Me gusta bailar.

items: With a verb use gusta (singular), also for several verbs: Me gusta cantar y bailar.
A mí, a ti, a él… are added for contrast or emphasis: A mí me gusta el té, pero a ella le gusta el café. Note a mí has an accent.
Names and nouns work the same way: A Pedro le gusta el fútbol. A mis padres les gustan los viajes.
Degree: Me gusta mucho / bastante / un poco. Negative: No me gusta nada el frío.

blocks.title: Think “is pleasing to me”
blocks.text: Dutch ik hou van katten / ik vind katten leuk becomes Me gustan los gatos: literally “cats are pleasing to me”. The cats are the subject, so the verb is plural: gustan.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
English
rows: Me encanta la música. Nos encantan los viajes.
I love music. We love travelling.
Me interesa la historia. Les interesan los coches.
History interests me. Cars interest them.

blocks.title: To love a person: querer
blocks.text: Encantar is for things and activities. For people use querer: Quiero a mi familia. Te quiero. (I love my family. I love you.)

rows: The thing liked is the subject. The person is me, te, le…
An infinitive always takes the singular gusta.
Llamarse already means “to be called”. No extra es.
A reflexive verb always needs its pronoun.
Body parts take the article, not a possessive.
A mi me gusta el té.
A mí me gusta el té.
After a preposition the pronoun is mí, with an accent.

blocks.text: Complete each sentence. Answers are on the last page.

items.full: Yo me levanto a las siete.
Ella se ducha por la mañana.
Nosotros nos acostamos a las once.
Ellos se sientan en el sofá.
A nosotros nos encantan los viajes.
A ti te gusta la música.

items.q: No me gusta el pescado. — A mí ______.
items.full: No me gusta el pescado. — A mí tampoco.
